```{=html}
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="r09" data-src="../assets/learn/data/r09-integrity-stakeholders.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r09-task:start (written by the test's --write mode from the data file; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Produce:</b> an integrity statement for your own study: funding and conflicts, contributions, data and licences, ethics and consent, stakeholders, corrections.</li>
<li><b>From:</b> six dilemmas, the norms behind them and the people your study affects.</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> the rubric's bar for integrity: licences checked, credit and conflicts stated, stakeholders treated fairly.</li></ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 30 minutes guided here, then about 30 minutes on your own statement.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Five norms</p><ul>
<li><b>Consent</b> (people agree, knowing what you will do): Tell survey participants how their answers will be used, and that they can say no. Get the ethics board's decision before the first interview.</li>
<li><b>Credit</b> (who did what, and whose work you used): List who did what, using contributor roles. Cite the dataset, not only the paper that describes it.</li>
<li><b>Conflicts of interest</b> (funding and ties, declared): State who funded the study and what they saw before publication. Declare that you advise the utility whose programme you evaluate.</li>
<li><b>Data licences</b> (the terms that come with data): Read the data agreement before you post a co-author's data. Keep the attribution line and the licence when you share an edited map layer.</li>
<li><b>Honest reporting</b> (all the results, and corrections): Report every scenario you ran, not only the best one. Ask the journal for a correction when you find an error.</li>
</ul>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Dilemma 1 · A funder wants a headline · Conflicts of interest</p>
<p>A regional utility association funds your study of a battery for Prairie Town. Across four scenarios, bills fall by 2 to 9% (illustrative). Its draft press release says “Batteries cut bills by 9%”.</p><ul>
<li>Agree: 9% is one of your results. <b>Hard to defend.</b> It reports the best case as the result. Letting a funder shape how results are reported is an unacceptable practice in the European code (§3.1).</li>
<li>Ask for “2 to 9%, depending on the scenario”, and name the funder in the paper and the release. <b>Defensible.</b> Accurate, with its range, and the support declared (§2.7). The funder still gets a usable sentence.</li>
<li>Decline to comment on the release. <b>Partly.</b> Your paper stays accurate, but the misleading number still goes out near your name. Better to correct it.</li>
</ul><p class="lx-hint">Source: ALLEA (2023), §2.7 and §3.1.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Dilemma 2 · A convenient scenario · Honest reporting</p>
<p>You ran eight scenarios. One shows a large benefit; seven show small ones. A co-author suggests presenting the large one as “the central case”.</p><ul>
<li>Present all eight, say how each was chosen, and give the range. <b>Defensible.</b> Honest reporting keeps the runs that weaken the story: negative results can be as relevant as positive ones (§2.7).</li>
<li>Put the large one in the main text and the other seven in a supplement. <b>Partly.</b> Everything is there, but the emphasis still misleads. Say in the main text that it is the outlier.</li>
<li>Present only the large one. <b>Hard to defend.</b> Omitting results without justification counts as falsification in the European code (§3.1).</li>
</ul><p class="lx-hint">Source: ALLEA (2023), §2.7 and §3.1.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Dilemma 3 · A co-author's data · Data licences</p>
<p>A co-author shared a rural co-op's hourly meter data with you under a data agreement. You want to post the data with your code so that others can rerun the study.</p><ul>
<li>Post it with the co-op's name removed. <b>Hard to defend.</b> A missing name does not override the agreement, and hourly meter data can still point to households.</li>
<li>Post it: the paper is out, so the data are public now. <b>Hard to defend.</b> Publication does not change the agreement. Posting may break it and expose the co-op's customers.</li>
<li>Read the agreement; post the code, a synthetic sample and how to request the data; cite the data and credit your co-author. <b>Defensible.</b> As open as possible, as closed as necessary, with the route to permission stated (§2.5).</li>
</ul><p class="lx-hint">Source: ALLEA (2023), §2.5 and §2.7.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Dilemma 4 · A community meeting · Working with stakeholders</p>
<p>Your model ranks three sites for a solar farm near Prairie Town (illustrative). At a public meeting, residents ask why their concern about losing farmland is not in the model.</p><ul>
<li>Say what the model includes and leaves out, record the concern, and report back how you treated it. <b>Defensible.</b> Fair process and recognition: the people affected are heard and can see what changed. Treating farmland could mean a new criterion or a sensitivity run.</li>
<li>Explain that the model is objective, so the ranking stands. <b>Hard to defend.</b> A ranking encodes choices about what counts. Calling it objective dismisses the people it affects.</li>
<li>Promise that the site they oppose will be dropped. <b>Hard to defend.</b> Researchers do not decide where farms go. A promise you cannot keep costs trust.</li>
</ul><p class="lx-hint">Source: Jenkins et al. (2016); ALLEA (2023), §2.4.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Dilemma 5 · A survey without consent · Consent</p>
<p>A student plans to survey renters door to door next week about their energy bills, recording names and addresses. No one has asked the <span class="lx-term" data-term="ethics-board">ethics board</span>.</p><ul>
<li>Go ahead: a short survey is harmless. <b>Hard to defend.</b> Research with people needs review first. Under DOE's order, even a survey that may be exempt needs the ethics board's determination (§4.a).</li>
<li>Go ahead, but do not record names. <b>Partly.</b> Collecting less is good practice, but review is still needed, and addresses identify people.</li>
<li>Pause; send the plan to the ethics board; add a consent statement; collect only what the question needs. <b>Defensible.</b> Prior review and informed consent (for DOE-supported research, DOE Order 443.1D, §4.a); participants told how their data will be used (§2.5).</li>
</ul><p class="lx-hint">Source: DOE Order 443.1D (2026), §4.a; ALLEA (2023), §2.4 and §2.5.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Dilemma 6 · An error after publication · Honest reporting</p>
<p>Months after publication you find a unit slip: one plant's capacity was entered in kW instead of MW. Fixing it changes your main result from 12% to 10% (illustrative).</p><ul>
<li>Fix it quietly in the code repository. <b>Partly.</b> Helpful, but the published record stays wrong. Do both.</li>
<li>Tell your co-authors and the journal promptly, and ask for a correction that says what changed. <b>Defensible.</b> Authors issue corrections promptly, and get credit for doing so (§2.7). The journal decides which kind of notice fits.</li>
<li>Say nothing: the conclusion still holds. <b>Hard to defend.</b> The published numbers are wrong, and others may reuse them.</li>
</ul><p class="lx-hint">Source: ALLEA (2023), §2.7.</p>
<!-- r09-task:end -->
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you sort the practices, choose an action in each dilemma before reading the norm, and write your own statement; your draft stays in this browser.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span>The dilemmas are fictional and set around Prairie Town; their numbers are illustrative, and no real person or organisation is described. The norms come from the primary sources listed below (checked on 3 November 2026). Rules on research with people differ by country, funder and institution: your own ethics board has the last word.</span></p>
```

## Two answers to the same task
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r09-exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r09-exemplars:start (written from the data file by LX.Exemplars' staticHTML in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak answer · Developing</p><p>The authors declare no competing interests [1]. Data available on request [2]. All participants agreed to take part [3]. All authors contributed equally [4].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> Funding is not mentioned at all, and an advisory role is a competing interest to declare.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> Which data, under which terms? Public data should be cited; restricted data need a stated route.</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> Agreement is not informed consent, and no ethics review is named.</li><li value="4"><b>Falls short:</b> It hides who did what; contributor roles make credit checkable.</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong answer · Proficient</p><p>Funding: a regional utility association funded the study; it saw the results one week before publication and could not change them [1]. Competing interests: one author advises the co-op on tariffs [2]. Contributions: A, conceptualization, formal analysis, writing (original draft); B, data curation, writing (review and editing) [3]. Data: EIA-930 (public domain, cited with its access date); the co-op's meter data under an agreement that does not allow sharing, so the code, a synthetic sample and the request route are public [4]. Ethics: the survey was reviewed by the university's ethics board before it began, and every participant gave informed consent [5]. Stakeholders: results were presented to residents and the co-op board before publication; their concerns are listed in an appendix [6]. Corrections: readers can report errors to the corresponding author, and any error that changes a result will go to the journal as a correction [7].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> The funder is named, with its role and its limits.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> An advisory tie is declared, not hidden.</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> Contributor roles make credit specific.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> Each source with its terms: as open as possible, as closed as necessary.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> Review before collection, and consent, both stated.</li><li value="6"><b>Works:</b> The people affected were heard, and readers can see how.</li><li value="7"><b>Works:</b> A route for errors, promised before anyone finds one.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<table class="lx-facts lx-ex-diff"><thead><tr><th scope="col"></th><th scope="col">Weak answer</th><th scope="col">Strong answer</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Funding</th><td>Not mentioned</td><td>Named, with what the funder could and could not do</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Data</th><td>“On request”</td><td>Each source with its terms and a route</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">People</th><td>“Agreed”</td><td>Ethics review, consent, and a report back</td></tr></tbody></table>
<!-- r09-exemplars:end -->
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Three questions</dt><dd>Does it involve people's data or participation? Someone else's work or data? Would readers conclude differently? Each yes adds a duty.</dd>
<dt>Who is owed what</dt><dd>The team is owed credit; the people a study is about are owed consent and a hearing; those who use or pay for it are owed all the results and the funding declared.</dd>
<dt>Write it down</dt><dd>An integrity statement turns the norms into lines a reader can check.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>Rules differ by place and funder</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>In the United States, research with people funded by federal agencies follows a common federal rule; the Department of Energy applies it through its order on human research subjects, built on the principles of the Belmont Report (1979): respect for persons, beneficence and justice.</li>
<li>In Europe, personal data in research fall under the General Data Protection Regulation, which the European code names when it asks researchers to tell participants how their data will be used (§2.5).</li>
<li>Journals add their own policies on authorship, competing interests and data availability: read them before you submit.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this studio leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>How to run interviews, focus groups or participatory workshops well: a qualitative-methods course, and a mentor, are the next step.</li>
<li>Misconduct investigations: the European code's §3.2 sets out how institutions handle them fairly.</li>
<li>Peer review: writing a review, and answering one point by point, is practised in the Researcher checkpoint (CK-R, upcoming).</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
